headline: Tōtoi is from Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, and is possibly derived from 太い (futoi, “fat”).
カーペット is from English carpet.
Chū, “inside”, is from Middle Chinese 中 (MC trjuwng).
セレモニー is borrowed from English ceremony.
Koisuru is 恋 (koi, “love”) plus する (-suru, “to do”).
スプリング is borrowed from English spring, and also clips スプリングコート (supuringu kōto, “a topcoat”).
Wakusei is a calque of Dutch dwaalster (“wander star”), 惑 (waku, “to move about confusedly, to wander”) plus 星 (sei, “star”), coined in 1792 by Motoki Yoshinaga.
Sangiin is 参議 (sangi, “participation in government”) plus 院 (-in, “institution”).
Kainyū is 介 (kai, “force in”) plus 入 (nyū, “enter”).
Shizuku is a kokuji, a character coined in Japan, combining 雨 (“rain”) plus 下 (“to drop”).
Musubitsuki is the nominative form of 結び付く (musubitsuku).
シック is from French chic.
Temawashi is a nominalization of 手で回す (te de mawasu, “to wind with the hand”), or the stem of 手回す (temawasu, “to prepare”).
In kappatsu, 発 is a daiyōji replacing 潑.
Seigi is from Middle Chinese 正義, and in the Meiji era it was repurposed to translate Western concepts of “justice”.
パート is borrowed from English part.
ルーズ is from English loose.
Shikiru is 仕 (shi, “do”) plus 切る (kiru, “cut off by a partition”).
In chinden, 殿 is a daiyōji replacing 澱.
Shutsuen is from Sinitic 出演 (chūyǎn).
Yakeni is やけ (yake) plus に (ni).
アプローチ is from English approach.
Tsutomete extends the regular verb form 務めて (tsutomete), from 務める (tsutomeru, “to make an effort, to work at something”).
チームワーク is from English teamwork.
Pekopeko is related to the verb 凹む (hekomu, “to become hollow or dented, to collapse inwardly, to sink in”).
Jibika is 耳鼻 (jibi, “ears and nose”) plus 科 (-ka, “field of study”).
セックス is borrowed from English sex.
Tenka is from Middle Chinese 天下 (MC then haeX, “heaven + under”), in the kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing.
スタイル is borrowed from English style.
Mesu, “to call”, is cognate with 見す (mesu, “(honorific) to see; to govern”).
Tanpakushitsu is 蛋白 (tanpaku, “egg white”) plus 質 (-shitsu, “material”), with 蛋白 a semantic loan from German Eiweiß.
